title: Simo Häyhä — the White Death of the Winter War
sources: Wikipedia: Simo Häyhä (17 December 1905 – 1 April 2002) — Finnish farmer and hunter from Rautjärvi, 160 cm tall, Civil Guard marksman; sniper in the 6th Company of JR 34 at the Battle of Kollaa in the Winter War; temperatures −40 to −20 °C; wore all-white camouflage while most Soviet troops had none; used an iron-sighted M/28-30 rifle rather than a scope (a scope means raising the head, fogs in the cold and can glint); kept snow in his mouth so his breath would not show and packed snow in front of his position to stop the muzzle blast stirring up snow; moved to his position before daybreak and stayed until after sunset; all kills in under 100 days; 25 kills on 21 December 1939; Finnish Army records: 259 sniper kills by 7 March 1940; his private memoir, written in 1940 and discovered in 2017, calls itself a 'sin list' and estimates around 500; historian Risto Marjomaa credits 'more than two hundred'; the nickname 'White Death' may come from Finnish propaganda; on 6 March 1940 an explosive bullet shattered his lower left jaw, he appeared dead and was placed on a pile of corpses until someone noticed his foot moving; regained consciousness on 13 March, the day peace was declared; read about his own death in a newspaper and wrote to correct it; asked in 1998 how he became so good, he answered 'Practice'; died 1 April 2002, aged 96
Wikipedia: Winter War — the Soviet Union invaded Finland on 30 November 1939; Battle of Kollaa, 7 December 1939 – 13 March 1940

Photos (public domain / CC0, Wikimedia Commons / Finnish Wartime Photograph Archive SA-kuva / Imperial War Museum): Simo Häyhä as a young soldier, in white camouflage with his honorary rifle (February 1940), in 1942; the M/28-30 'Pystykorva' rifle; the Kollaa front; Finnish ski patrols and soldiers in the snow; a Swedish newspaper on Häyhä, 1940
Archive film (public domain): Why We Fight: The Battle of Russia (US War Department, 1943) — Soviet troops and fighting in winter, 1941–42 — illustrative, not the Winter War itself

post.facebook:
In under 100 days, a quiet Finnish farmer became — by most counts — the deadliest sniper in history.

Simo Häyhä stood 5 ft 3 and grew up hunting near the Russian border. When the Soviet Union invaded Finland in November 1939, he was sent to Kollaa, where the cold fell to −40 °C. He dressed in white, used a rifle with iron sights and no scope, kept snow in his mouth so his breath wouldn't show, and went out before dawn and came back after dark.

The Finnish Army confirmed 259 kills with his rifle. His private memoir, found in 2017, says around 500 — he called it his "sin list". Some historians doubt it and say just over 200.

On 6 March 1940 an explosive bullet tore through his face. Thought dead, he was laid on a pile of bodies until someone saw his foot move. He woke a week later — on the day the war ended — and later read about his own death in the paper.

He lived to 96. Asked how he got so good, he said one word: "Practice."

Legend or propaganda? ❄️

#History #WinterWar #SimoHayha #WhiteDeath

Simo Häyhä fought at Kollaa in the Winter War of 1939–40 at −40 °C, with an iron-sighted rifle and no scope. The Finnish Army confirmed 259 kills with his rifle; his own memoir, found in 2017, estimates around 500 — his "sin list". Some historians say just over 200.
